title: What If You Set Camels Loose in a Desert? Australia Did, and Got a Million of Them

scenes.text: What if you set camels loose in a desert? Australia did. Now it shoots them from helicopters.
British settlers shipped camels to Australia from 1840 to haul supplies. Then cars arrived, and in the 1920s the camels were let go.
No lions, no wolves, endless scrub. The herd grew up to ten percent a year. By 2009, about one million roamed the outback.
In droughts they flatten fences, foul waterholes, and have ripped apart air conditioners to get at the water inside.
From 2009 to 2013, shooters in helicopters culled about 160,000. Another 100,000 starved in one desert. Numbers halved.
Then they bounced back to over a million. A pack animal nobody wanted became a million-strong wild herd. Still growing.

description:
What if camels were set loose in a desert? British settlers brought camels to Australia from 1840 as pack animals, then released them into the interior in the 1920s and 1930s once motor vehicles took over.
With no natural predators the population can grow up to 10 percent a year; a 2009 estimate put it at about one million animals across 3.3 million square kilometres. They knock down fences, foul water sources and in the 2019 drought broke into air conditioners for water. A national cull from 2009 to 2013 removed about 160,000 camels by aerial shooting and halved the population to roughly 300,000, but it has since rebounded to over a million, costing an estimated 11.5 million dollars a year in damage and control.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: A 2016 study found a camel meat industry would need to take 14,000 animals a year just to be viable. Which animal would take over if we let it loose? Drop your own what-if below.
